items.prose: Fair £1 bets, stopping at £0 or £20. First-step analysis gives $D_i = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2} D_{i+1} + \tfrac{1}{2} D_{i-1}$ with $D_0 = D_{20} = 0$.
items.question: Write the expected number of bets $D_i$ as an expression in $i$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The solution vanishes at both ends and has second difference $-2$.

byKey.product: $20i$ is not 0 at $i = 20$. The game from £20 is already over.
byKey.square: $i^2$ is not 0 at $i = 20$. It must vanish at both ends.
byKey.prob: $\tfrac{i}{20}$ is the chance of reaching £20, not the number of bets.

explain.text: Try $D_i = i(20 - i)$: it is 0 at both ends. And $1 + \tfrac{1}{2}[(i+1)(19-i) + (i-1)(21-i)] = 1 + (20i - i^2 - 1) = i(20 - i)$, so it solves the equation. From £10 the game lasts 100 bets on average.

items.prose: A signal is right 70% of the time. Each trade makes £1 when it is right and loses £1 when it is wrong, independently.
items.question: Write $\mathrm{Var}(S_n)$, the variance of the P&L after $n$ trades, as an expression in $n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One trade has variance $1 - (2p - 1)^2$.

byKey.coin: $0.21n$ is $np(1 - p)$, the variance for 0-or-1 outcomes. A $\pm$£1 trade is twice as wide: multiply by 4.
byKey.fair: $n$ is the fair walk's variance. The 70% hit rate shrinks each trade's variance to $1 - 0.4^2$.
byKey.mean: $0.4n$ is the mean P&L. The question asks for the variance.

explain.text: One trade has mean $2(0.7) - 1 = 0.4$ and variance $1 - 0.4^2 = 0.84$. Independent trades add, so $\mathrm{Var}(S_n) = 0.84n$. The mean, $0.4n$, overtakes the sd, $\sqrt{0.84n}$, after just a few trades.

items.title: The unfair ruin formula
items.prose: Each bet wins with chance $p \ne \tfrac{1}{2}$; let $q = 1 - p$ and $r = q/p$. As before, $P_0 = 0$ and $P_N = 1$.
items.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: First step: $P_i = p P_{i+1} + q P_{i-1}$ for $0 < i < N$.
Write $P_i = (p + q) P_i$ and rearrange: $p(P_{i+1} - P_i)$ equals $q(P_i - P_{i-1})$, so each gap is $r$ times the one before.
Add the first $i$ gaps: $P_i = P_1 (1 + r + \dots + r^{i-1})$, a geometric sum equal to $P_1 \tfrac{1 - r^i}{1 - r}$ since $r \ne 1$.
Use $P_N = 1$: $P_1 = \tfrac{1 - r}{1 - r^N}$, so $P_i = \tfrac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N}$.

feedback.correct: First step, gap ratio, gaps as powers, geometric sum, boundary.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The fair proof had equal gaps; here each gap is $r$ times the last.

explain.text: The first-step equation says the gaps grow by the factor $r = q/p$. Summing a geometric series of gaps and fixing $P_N = 1$ gives the formula. As $p \to \tfrac{1}{2}$, $r \to 1$ and it tends to $i/N$, the fair answer.

items.prose: Paths of $\pm 1$ steps go from $(0, 0)$ to $(10, 2)$.
items.question: How many of them never touch level 4?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count all paths to $(10, 2)$, then subtract those that touch 4.

byKey.touch: 45 is the number that do touch 4. Subtract it from the total.
byKey.all: 210 counts every path to $(10, 2)$, including those that reach 4.
byKey.wrong-mirror: Check the mirror end: $2m - k = 2 \times 4 - 2 = 6$, and $\binom{10}{8} = 45$ paths reach $(10, 6)$.

explain.text: There are $\binom{10}{6} = 210$ paths to $(10, 2)$. Those touching 4 match the paths to $(10, 6)$, of which there are $\binom{10}{8} = 45$. So $210 - 45 = 165$ stay below 4 throughout.

items.title: First passage at step 9
items.prose: A fair walk starts at 0. Let $T$ be the first step at which it reaches 3. To have $T = 9$, the walk must sit at 2 at step 8 without having touched 3, then step up.
items.question: What is $P(T = 9)$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count paths to $(8, 2)$ that never touch 3, then multiply by the chance of the final up step.

byKey.end-at-3: $\tfrac{84}{512}$ is $P(S_9 = 3)$. Many of those paths reached 3 before step 9.
byKey.no-avoid: $\tfrac{56}{512}$ uses every path to $(8, 2)$. Some of them touched 3 already; remove them by reflection.
byKey.by-8: That is the chance of being at 2 at step 8, $\tfrac{56}{256}$, before removing paths that touched 3 or taking the last step.

explain.text: Paths to $(8, 2)$ number $\binom{8}{5} = 56$. Those touching 3 reflect to $(8, 4)$: $\binom{8}{6} = 28$. So 28 paths avoid 3, and with the final up step $P(T = 9) = \tfrac{28}{2^9} \approx 0.0547$.

items.prose: A roulette bet on red wins with chance $\tfrac{18}{37}$ and pays even money. You have £10, bet £1 at a time and stop at £20 or £0.
items.question: What is the chance you reach £20? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: About 0.368: the 2.7% house edge costs 13 points over the game.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $r = \tfrac{19}{18}$ with $i = 10$ and $N = 20$.

byKey.fair: 0.5 ignores the zero on the wheel, which tilts every bet.
byKey.single: 0.4865 is one bet on red. That is the bold play: one £10 bet gives this.
byKey.flip: 0.6320 is the chance of going broke.

explain.text: $r = 19/18 \approx 1.0556$ and $r^{10} \approx 1.717$, so $P_{10} = \tfrac{1}{1 + r^{10}} \approx 0.368$. One bold bet of £10 would give $\tfrac{18}{37} \approx 0.486$. Against a house edge, fewer bets are better.

items.title: Exact barrier chance for any p
items.prose: Reflection only works for fair steps. Dynamic programming works for any $p$: track the chance of each position among paths that have not yet hit $m$, one step at a time. When a step reaches $m$, move that probability into `hit`.
items.question: Complete `touch_prob(n, m, p)`.

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests, fair and biased, with exact answers. Each is accepted when math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9).

feedback.correct: Exact for any $p$, and it agrees with reflection when $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. For each position, send probability $p$ up and $1 - p$ down; anything reaching $m$ goes into `hit`.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace the `...` with the two moves.

explain.text: Each pass moves every surviving probability one step and absorbs what reaches $m$. For $p = 0.5$ it reproduces 0.34375, the reflection answer. For $p = 0.55$ it gives 0.4523, where reflection would wrongly give 0.5321.

items.title: Prove and use the reflection principle
items.prompt:
A trader's daily P&L is a fair walk: $S_0 = 0$ and each day adds $\pm$£1k with equal chance, independently.

1. Prove that for a level $m \ge 1$, $$\begin{aligned} &P\left(\max_{j \le n} S_j \ge m\right) \\ &= P(S_n \ge m) + P(S_n > m). \end{aligned}$$ Define the reflection map and show it is a one-to-one pairing.
2. A take-profit order closes the book if the P&L touches $+$£5k within 20 days. Find the chance it triggers, given $P(S_{20} \ge 6) = 0.13159$.
3. Explain why the formula fails if each day wins with chance $p = 0.55$, and say how you would compute the chance then.
items.model:
**1. Proof.** Every path of $n$ fair steps has probability $2^{-n}$, so probabilities are counts over $2^n$. Split $A = \{\max_{j \le n} S_j \ge m\}$ into $A_1 = \{S_n \ge m\}$ and $A_2 = \{\max_{j \le n} S_j \ge m,\ S_n < m\}$. Every path in $\{S_n \ge m\}$ is in $A$, since it is at or above $m$ at step $n$, so $P(A_1) = P(S_n \ge m)$.

For a path in $A_2$ let $\tau$ be the first step with $S_\tau = m$; it exists because the path reaches $m$. Define the reflected path by $S'_j = S_j$ for $j \le \tau$ and $S'_j = 2m - S_j$ for $j > \tau$: every step after $\tau$ is flipped. Its end is $2m - S_n > m$, because $S_n < m$.

The map is one to one and onto $\{S_n > m\}$. The prefix up to $\tau$ is unchanged, so $\tau$ is also the first touch of the new path; reflecting again after $\tau$ gives back the original. Conversely, any path with $S_n > m$ must pass through $m$, since steps are $\pm 1$ and it starts at $0 < m$. Reflecting it after its first touch gives a path in $A_2$. Equal counts give $P(A_2) = P(S_n > m)$, and $P(A) = P(A_1) + P(A_2)$.

**2. Take-profit.** With $n = 20$, $m = 5$: $S_{20}$ is even, so $P(S_{20} \ge 5) = P(S_{20} > 5) = P(S_{20} \ge 6) = 0.13159$. The chance is $2 \times 0.13159 = 0.26318$, about 26%.

**3. Drift.** With $p = 0.55$ paths are no longer equally likely. A segment after $\tau$ with $u$ ups and $d$ downs has probability $p^u q^d$; its reflection has $p^d q^u$. They differ unless $u = d$, so the pairing matches path counts but not probabilities, and the formula overstates the chance (here it would give 0.504 instead of 0.410). Compute it exactly by dynamic programming over positions with an absorbing level at $m$, or by a seeded simulation. Weighting each reflected path by $(q/p)^{S_n - m}$ also repairs the formula: $P(\max \ge m) = P(S_n \ge m) + E\big[(q/p)^{S_n - m};\ S_n > m\big]$.

rubric.text: Notes that fair paths are equally likely, so probabilities are counts over $2^n$.
Splits the event by whether $S_n \ge m$ or $S_n < m$, and shows the first part is $P(S_n \ge m)$.
Defines the first touch $\tau$ and the reflection $S'_j = 2m - S_j$ for $j > \tau$, with end $2m - S_n > m$.
Shows the map is a bijection onto $\{S_n > m\}$: same first touch, inverse by reflecting again, and every path ending above $m$ passes $m$.
Uses parity to get $P(S_{20} \ge 5) = P(S_{20} > 5) = 0.13159$ and answers about 0.263.
Explains that with $p \ne \tfrac{1}{2}$ a path and its reflection have different probabilities.
Gives a working method for the biased case: dynamic programming, simulation, or the $(q/p)^{S_n - m}$ weighting.

items.prose: A strategy wins £1 on 52% of trades and loses £1 on the rest. After $n$ trades its P&L has mean $0.04n$ and sd $\sqrt{4n \times 0.52 \times 0.48}$.
items.question: About how many trades until the mean P&L is 2 standard deviations above zero?

byKey.linear: 50 is $\sqrt{n}$. Square it to get the number of trades.
byKey.one-sd: 624 trades put the mean only 1 standard deviation above zero. Two needs four times as many.
byKey.thousand: After 1,000 trades the mean is only 1.27 standard deviations above zero.

explain.text: Set $0.04n = 2\sqrt{0.9984 n}$. Then $\sqrt{n} = 2\sqrt{0.9984}/0.04 \approx 49.96$ and $n \approx 2496$. The mean grows like $n$ but the noise like $\sqrt{n}$, so a small edge needs thousands of trades to show.
